certainty_reasoning: Cook documents a forty-one-year household bond - Bloodworth, 'a teenage footballer', moved into Ives's Adelaide Road house in 1909 and stayed until Ives's death in 1950, one of the working-class men Ives called his 'children' in a household Cook twice marks as unconventional - but stops short of any sexual or romantic characterization. Lewis (podcast) likewise speaks only of 'domestic relationships' with 'a succession of younger men'. The lover reading comes from the project's research leads (Lewis interview prep), which are not citable; hence alleged, pending the Ives diaries or Lewis's published work. CORROBORATION (2026-08-03): Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. That sharpens the evidence but does not lift the class: it remains one historian's careful inference, and he does not assert sexual relations outright. EVIDENCE-TIER CORRECTION 2026-08-03 (): reclassified to self-reported. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.
date_label: Moved into the Adelaide Road household 1909; stayed until Ives's death, 1950 (Cook).
summary: Harold Bloodworth ('Pug'), described by Cook as 'a teenage footballer', moved into Ives's Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill household in 1909 and remained for the rest of Ives's life - the longest-staying of the working- and lower-middle-class men Ives paternalistically called his 'children'. The sources read document the household, not a sexual bond; the characterization of Bloodworth as a lover awaits first-person evidence from the Ives diaries.

disputed.claim: That Bloodworth was one of Ives's lovers, beyond being a member of his household from 1909 to 1950
disputed.asserted_by: Project research leads (interview prep drawing on Brian Lewis's account of Ives), which gloss Ives's household 'children', including Bloodworth ('Pug'), as his lovers
disputed.grounds: No citable source read so far asserts it. Cook (2003), p. 148, documents membership and duration in an 'unconventional household' without romantic or sexual characterization; Lewis on the podcast describes 'domestic relationships' with 'a succession of younger men' without naming Bloodworth or stating a sexual bond. Resolution requires the Ives diaries (Harry Ransom Center) or Lewis's forthcoming biography.

sources.quote: When Pug and another long term resident Cubby (Charles Gee) were both away he wrote in his diary: 'I feel sad. I love those two, deeply, tenderly [...] Love's quite different from passion [...] to sleep side by side with one's comrade is beyond all worlds beautiful. Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'.
sources.context: Cook quoting Ives's diary (vol. 76, 20 January 1921, p. 25, per Cook's endnote 35) on Pug and Cubby being away; the ellipses are Cook's own
sources.supports: Ives's own diary on sleeping beside Pug (Bloodworth) and Cubby - 'those two' names both men; participant testimony, quoted by Cook from Diary vol. 76. QUOTE EXTENDED by the Q2 quality pass 2026-08-03: the record previously stopped at 'beyond all worlds beautiful', cutting the clause in which Ives actually says what the intimacy gave him - 'Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'. That clause is the most explicit first-hand characterization of this bond anywhere in the sources read, and it is the sentence that distinguishes what Ives had with these men from what the word 'lover' would imply: he names love, disclaims passion, and locates the value in comfort.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 112 (printed folio 101 confirmed on the rendered page), read as page image 2026-08-03; re-read in the source and the quotation extended to its full printed extent 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: …in the diary for the post-1905 period there is a sense of Ives settling down - not to a 'conventional' family, but with a series of working- and lower-middle-class men whom he paternalistically referred to as his 'children'. Kit brought his wife and children to live there for a while, and in 1909, Harold Bloodworth, a teenage footballer, moved in and stayed until Ives' death in 1950.
sources.context: Cook, on Ives's Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill household (from 1905)
sources.supports: Bloodworth entered the household in 1909 as 'a teenage footballer' and stayed until Ives's death in 1950; the household's 'children' framing
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 164, printed folio 148 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Sentence opening ('Adelaide Road was, according to historian Donald Olsen, "the essence of suburbia", and') elided; full passage transcribed in dossier.

sources.quote: He moved from the countryside into London, lived in London for most of his life, mostly in a suburban house in North London, where he lived with a succession of younger men who sometimes stayed for just a few years, sometimes they stayed for decades.
sources.context: Brian Lewis, spoken in a National Humanities Center podcast interview about Ives; ASR transcript, wording may vary slightly from the audio
sources.supports: The household pattern - Bloodworth is the stayed-for-decades case, though Lewis names no one; Lewis frames these as 'domestic relationships' and elsewhere notes Ives's 'relationships were all with adults'
sources.provenance: Repo ASR transcript docs/research/queer-history/victorian/ives/audio/Discovery & Inspiration - Brian Lewis, "George Cecil Ives and the Transformation of Discourses on Sexuality".txt, read 2026-08-03; verified against the transcript file, not the audio.

sources.context: The character of the Ives-Bloodworth relationship as recorded first-person across the 1909-1949 diary volumes
sources.supports: Whether Bloodworth was a lover rather than solely a household member ('child') cannot be said for sure with the sources at hand. This stays unconfirmed pending an archive visit - the volumes themselves at the Harry Ransom Center.

sources.quote: Though Ives' relationships with the other men at Adelaide Road possibly started sexually, they seem quickly to have become platonic - even though he continued to sleep with them from time to time.
sources.context: Cook's summary characterization of the Adelaide Road household relationships
sources.supports: Cook's own careful reading: a possible sexual beginning, a platonic settling, continued bed-sharing throughout.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 112 (printed folio 101 confirmed on the rendered page), read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: The men thus shifted from (possible) lovers to sons and, in bed, to comrades.
sources.context: Cook, immediately after quoting Ives's diary on sleeping beside Pug and Cubby
sources.supports: The trajectory Cook proposes for these relationships.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 112 (printed folio 101 confirmed on the rendered page), read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: The two men he was living with - Harold Bloodworth and Stanley Saunders (Pug and Elephant) - were left the Adelaide Road house and contents; Tilly Hayes was next in line to inherit after them.
sources.context: Cook, on the provisions of Ives's will (made October 1939 per Cook's text; dated 1 December 1939 per his endnote 80)
sources.supports: The strongest single statement of Bloodworth's standing in the household: he and Saunders inherit the house itself. Ives's own ranking of his attachments, in a legal document.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pp. 120-121 (printed folios 109 and 110 confirmed on the rendered pages; the sentence runs across the page break), read as page images 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: If conventionally there might be a single spouse, Ives recognised the three-way affections between himself and the men he lived with. Bloodworth, who had lived with Ives at this point for around 30 years, was also appointed one of his executors.
sources.context: Cook's gloss on the will's treatment of the household
sources.supports: Cook explicitly frames the Ives/Bloodworth/Saunders triad against the spousal model - the nearest he comes to calling it a partnership, though 'affections' is not a claim of sexual relations. Independently corroborates the 1909 start date already in this record: 'around 30 years' before the 1939 will.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 121 (printed folio 110 confirmed on the rendered page), read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: While a late night for Pug left Ives feeling 'pretty sure he had arranged to stay with a girl', he observed that 'a wise parent does not ask too many questions' (even though usually 'we have no secrets between us').
sources.context: Cook, on Ives as paterfamilias at Adelaide Road; all three inner quotations are Ives's, from the diary (vol. 76, 2 October 1920, p. 49, per Cook's endnote 30)
sources.supports: The clearest first-hand statement of the terms Ives set for this relationship, and the one that bears directly on the disputed block above: Ives knows Bloodworth spends nights with women, casts himself as parent rather than partner, and declines to ask - while still claiming 'we have no secrets between us'. Ives's diary, vol. 76, 2 October 1920, as quoted by Cook. Read against the lead quotation, the two together give the shape of the bond in Ives's own terms: love and a shared bed, without exclusivity and without the vocabulary of coupledom.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 112 (printed folio 101 confirmed on the rendered page), read as page image 2026-08-03.
